meta.title: Who originally recorded "Rivers of Babylon"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Boney M. The Melodians recorded it in Jamaica in 1970 for Leslie Kong; Boney M.’s disco version came in 1978.
meta.ogDescription: Boney M. had the 1978 megahit, but The Melodians cut it in 1970 for Leslie Kong’s Beverley’s label in Kingston.

answer.label: Not a Boney M. original — The Melodians recorded it in Jamaica in 1970
answer.originalArtistDates: Jamaican rocksteady and reggae vocal group, formed in Greenwich Town, Kingston, in 1963
answer.sourceLine: Boney M.’s 1978 disco version is one of the best-selling singles in British history, and most listeners file the song as a Euro-disco creation. It is a cover. “Rivers of Babylon” was written by Brent Dowe and Trevor McNaughton of the Jamaican group The Melodians and recorded by them in 1970 for producer Leslie Kong’s Beverley’s label. The Jamaican government initially banned it as subversive because of its Rastafarian framing; once the ban was lifted it took three weeks to reach number one in Jamaica, and the soundtrack to the 1972 film The Harder They Come carried it to the rest of the world.

original.heading: Who recorded it first
original.label: Leslie Kong production (Beverley's)
original.released: Recorded in 1970 in Kingston for producer Leslie Kong and issued on his Beverley’s Records label; it is also the title track of The Melodians’ 1970 Beverley’s album, catalogue BLP 019.
original.charted: A number one in Jamaica — it reached the top within three weeks once the government ban on it was lifted. It did not chart internationally in its own right; the 1972 soundtrack album carried it abroad.
original.cover: Boney M., released 3 April 1978 on Hansa (West Germany), Sire (US) and Atlantic (UK), produced by Frank Farian. Number one in the UK and across much of Europe, No. 30 on the US Billboard Hot 100, and over a million UK copies sold.
trail: The song was written and recorded in 1970 by Brent Dowe and Trevor McNaughton of The Melodians, with lyrics adapted from Psalms 137 and 19 — see Wikipedia’s article on the song ↗.
The Jamaican government initially banned the record for its Rastafarian references; once lifted, it took three weeks to top the Jamaican chart, per the same Wikipedia article ↗.
The 1970 Jamaican pressing on Leslie Kong’s Beverley’s Records, catalogue BLP 019, is catalogued at MusicBrainz ↗, with the title track at 2:51.
Boney M.’s cover followed on 3 April 1978 on Hansa, Sire and Atlantic, with Frank Farian and George Reyam added to the writing credit — Boney M. on Wikipedia ↗.

authors.name: The Melodians
authors.heading: The Melodians
authors.metaLine: Jamaican vocal group, formed Kingston 1963 · Brent Dowe, Trevor McNaughton, Tony Brevett
authors.bio: The Melodians were formed in the Greenwich Town area of Kingston in 1963 by Tony Brevett, Brent Dowe and Trevor McNaughton, and became one of the great harmony groups of the rocksteady era. Their biggest record was made for producer Leslie Kong at Beverley’s, and “Rivers of Babylon” became an anthem of the Rastafari movement. Its inclusion on the soundtrack of The Harder They Come ↗ in 1972 turned a Jamaican hit into an international one. Kong died in 1971, and the group afterwards recorded for other producers including Lee Perry and Byron Lee’s Dynamic Studios.

authors.name: Boney M.
authors.heading: Boney M.
authors.metaLine: West German vocal group, formed 1974 by producer Frank Farian
authors.bio: Boney M. were assembled in West Germany in 1974 by producer Frank Farian, fronted by Liz Mitchell, Marcia Barrett, Maizie Williams and Bobby Farrell. Their “Rivers of Babylon” was issued on 3 April 1978 and went to number one across most of Europe, selling over a million copies in the UK alone and becoming one of that country’s all-time best-selling singles. The record is a genuinely inspired reworking — the only error is chronological. Farian and George Reyam were added to the songwriting credit for the Boney M. arrangement, alongside Dowe and McNaughton.

authors.name: Brent Dowe and Trevor McNaughton
authors.heading: Brent Dowe & Trevor McNaughton
authors.metaLine: Jamaican singers and songwriters; Dowe died 2006, McNaughton died 2018
authors.bio: Dowe and McNaughton wrote “Rivers of Babylon” as members of The Melodians, adapting the texts of Psalms 137 and 19 into a Rastafari song. McNaughton had conceived the group and recruited its members; Dowe shared lead vocals with Tony Brevett and left for a solo career in 1973 before rejoining. Dowe died of a heart attack in January 2006 at the age of 59. McNaughton, the last surviving original member, died on 20 November 2018 at 77.

misattribution.heading: Right song, wrong origin story
misattribution.intro: The Boney M. single is so large in European memory that the Jamaican record underneath it disappears. Here is what the sources actually say.

items.why: Their version, released 3 April 1978 and produced by Frank Farian, topped charts across Europe and sold over a million copies in the UK — but it is a cover of a Jamaican record.
Recorded in 1970 for producer Leslie Kong at Beverley’s in Kingston. Banned in Jamaica, then a Jamaican number one within three weeks of the ban being lifted.
Both were members of The Melodians. Frank Farian and George Reyam were added to the credit for the Boney M. arrangement, which is part of why the song reads as European.
The Melodians’ recording reached an international audience through the Island soundtrack album to the 1972 film — the route by which the song got to Europe at all.

misattribution.truthLine: Boney M. made it enormous. The Melodians made it.

context.heading: Why the cover swallowed the original
lead: The Melodians’ record was never obscure — it was a Jamaican number one and it opened a globally distributed film soundtrack. What it lacked was European radio. Boney M. arrived on a continental pop machine built by Frank Farian, with a Hansa/Atlantic release, a television-ready group and an arrangement engineered for the 1978 discotheque. That record sold in numbers that simply rewrite public memory: over a million UK copies, one of the ten best-selling British singles ever pressed.

There is a second reason the authorship blurred. Farian and George Reyam were added to the writing credit for the Boney M. version, so the label copy that reached millions of European buyers carried German names next to the Jamaican ones. Combined with a sound that gave no audible clue of rocksteady origin, the song arrived in Europe looking like something that had been made there.
detailsBody: 1963 — The Melodians form in Greenwich Town, Kingston: Tony Brevett, Brent Dowe, Trevor McNaughton.
1970 — Dowe and McNaughton write “Rivers of Babylon”, adapting Psalms 137 and 19. The Melodians record it for Leslie Kong at Beverley’s.

1970 — The Jamaican government bans the record as subversive; after the ban is lifted it reaches number one in Jamaica within three weeks. It is also the title track of the group’s Beverley’s album, catalogue BLP 019.
1971 — Leslie Kong dies; the group moves to other producers.
1972 — The Melodians’ recording appears on the Island soundtrack album to the film The Harder They Come, reaching an international audience.

3 April 1978 — Boney M. release their version on Hansa, Sire and Atlantic, produced by Frank Farian, with Farian and George Reyam added to the writing credit. It tops charts across Europe and passes a million UK copies.
context.pull: A Jamaican number one that the discotheque re-issued as its own invention.

listen.what: The Melodians’ Leslie Kong–produced recording, as issued on The Harder They Come
listen.source: An auto-generated upload on the “The Melodians - Topic” channel; the description reads “Provided to YouTube by Universal Music Group” and carries a ℗ 1970 Island Records line, crediting Leslie Kong as producer. Its running time of 4:15 matches the MusicBrainz entry for the Harder They Come soundtrack cut (4:19), not the shorter 2:51 Beverley’s album cut — it is the same period recording in its soundtrack form, not a later re-recording.
